analysis.investment_thesis: Allied Blenders posted near-zero profits for four consecutive years (FY21-FY24: INR 1–3 Cr annually) before a single-year jump to INR 195 Cr in FY25, yet trades at 59.8x P/E and 33x EV/EBITDA — a valuation that demands sustained growth that a 3.3% revenue CAGR business has not earned. The spirits sector has appeal, but ABDL's execution history fails Fisher's management quality test.
key_strengths: Officer's Choice is India's largest-selling whisky by volume — genuine brand scale and distribution reach across price-sensitive mass market
ROE of 20% and ROCE of 21.1% in FY25 are Fisher-quality returns, but are based on the post-IPO equity base and the anomalous profit jump
Finance costs declining (8% CAGR reduction) while EBITDA is recovering — balance sheet is cleaner than peers
key_risks: Revenue CAGR of just 3.3% over 5 years is completely inconsistent with Fisher's 20%+ growth standard; real volume growth is even lower given inflation
P/E of 59.8x and EV/EBITDA of 33.4x price in perfection that the company's track record does not justify — four years of near-zero profits followed by one good year is not a growth franchise
State government excise policy is the dominant driver of profitability in Indian spirits — this regulatory dependency represents a fundamental limit on pricing power and margin control
red_flags: Net profit was INR 1–3 Cr for FY21, FY22, FY23, FY24 — effectively zero for four years; FY25's INR 195 Cr surge is likely driven by IPO-related accounting or one-time items, not operational improvement
OCF turned sharply negative in FY25 (-INR 678 Cr) after being positive in prior years — a major reversal coinciding with the IPO year raises questions about working capital and cash quality
Promoter holding at 80.91% leaves very limited free float; this concentration creates governance concerns and market illiquidity
analysis.detailed_analysis:
From the scuttlebutt perspective, the Indian mass spirits market is heavily state-controlled — excise duties, distribution licenses, and price controls are set by 30+ state governments, each with different rules. This makes building a compounding growth business exceptionally difficult. ABDL's Officer's Choice brand has tremendous volume, but volume leadership in a price-controlled market does not translate into pricing power or margin expansion. The five-year record of near-zero profits confirms this.

The FY25 profit of INR 195 Cr coinciding with the IPO and a massive equity base expansion (from INR 407 Cr to INR 1,558 Cr) followed by a negative OCF of -INR 678 Cr is a pattern I find deeply suspicious. Fisher demands businesses where management has demonstrated the ability to grow earnings consistently — ABDL has done the opposite. At 59.8x P/E, this is priced as a quality compounder; the fundamentals tell a different story.
